newsitem.title: USA: Spermicide film does not halt AIDS, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Spermicide film does not halt AIDS, study finds.

text.p: In a setback to the search for an anti-AIDS microbicide for women, scientists said on Thursday that a contraceptive film containing a common spermicide does not block transmission of the AIDS virus or several other sexually transmitted diseases.

Public health workers and scientists have been searching for microbicides to protect women against AIDS, preferably in a way that women could control even in societies where they have less autonomy. Condoms do not provide perfect protection, and men are not always willing to use them.

A two-year study in Cameroon, conducted with the backing of the U.S. National Institutes of Health, showed that the spermicide nonoxynol-9 (N-9) in film form did not block the AIDS virus. Nor did it give the women protection against gonorrhea or chlamydia.

"We had hoped that the N-9 film might increase a woman's available options for HIV and STD protection," said Dr. Willard Cates, of Family Health International, a nonprofit group that helped carry out the study.
"These results show that we must accelerate our research programmes dedicated to finding new products and techniques for women to use."

The chemical does kill the HIV virus in the test tube, and studies are ongoing about whether it is effective against the virus in other topical forms. There is some evidence that it might irritate or disrupt cells in the genital tract, making women more vulnerable to infection.
The study tracked nearly 1,300 female sex workers, 941 of whom completed a year follow-up. All the women were given counselling, condoms and treated for other sexually-transmitted diseases (STDs).

Half the women were given vaginal film containing the spermicide nonoxynol-9, and half were given a placebo film. But the AIDS transmission rate of 6.7 percent was the same in both groups, indicating that the spermicide did not fight AIDS.
The counselling, condoms and medical treatment did reduce AIDS infection in both groups, since the rate among sex workers in Cameroon is about twice that rate.

"We are encouraged by the apparent effectiveness of overall intervention programme that including counselling, STD treatment and encouragement of condom use," said Rodney Hoff, a researcher on AIDS prevention at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases.
